terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Run your file here to see the morning count.

tasks.title: Name the shop
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1` in `src/variables.js`, make a `const` called `shopName` that holds the text `Wickhollow Candles`, then print it.

Check runs your file and reads `shopName`: it must hold exactly that text and be made with `const`.
nextSteps: Make the variable with `const`, the name, `=` and the text in quotes.
Print it with `console.log` on the next line.
Run `node src/variables.js` and read the output.
hints: A variable is made with a keyword, a name and a value. The lesson shows one for the kettle.
The name never changes, which tells you which keyword to use. The value is text, so it needs quotes.
The line has the shape `const shopName = '...'`, with the shop's name where the dots are.

tasks.title: Count the cedar candles
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, make a `let` called `cedarOnShelf`. It starts with the number of cedar candles delivered this morning, which is in `cedarDelivered` near the top of the file. Print it.

Check runs your file with other delivery numbers in place of the ones at the top, so `cedarOnShelf` has to be built on the name `cedarDelivered`, not on a number you type.
nextSteps: Read the two lines under "This morning's numbers".
Give it the value of `cedarDelivered` by writing that name.
Print it and run the file.
hints: A variable can start with the value of another variable, not only with a number or text you type.
The count will change later today, which tells you which keyword to use. On the right of `=`, write the name of the variable that holds the delivery.
The line has the shape `let cedarOnShelf = ...`, with the delivery's variable name where the dots are.

tasks.title: Sell some candles
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, `cedarSold` candles were sold this morning. Give `cedarOnShelf` a new value: the number left on the shelf after the sale. Then print it again.

Check runs your file with other numbers at the top and reads `cedarOnShelf` at the end. It also reads your file to see that Task 3 gives the existing variable a new value, rather than making a new one.
nextSteps: Make sure Task 2 passes first: Task 3 changes the same variable.
Under `// Task 3`, start a line with the name `cedarOnShelf` and `=`.
On the right, take `cedarSold` away from what is on the shelf now.
Print it again and run the file: you should see two different counts.
hints: You are not making a new variable here. You are changing one you already made.
Giving a variable a new value is its name, `=` and the new value, with no keyword in front. The right side can use the variable's own current value.
The line has the shape `cedarOnShelf = cedarOnShelf - ...`, with the sold candles' variable where the dots are.

tasks.title: Give x and y real names
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 4`, two variables are called `x` and `y`, and nobody can tell what they hold. Rename `x` to `packerName` and `y` to `emailerName`, everywhere they appear. Their values stay the same.

Check runs your file and reads `packerName` and `emailerName`, and makes sure `x` and `y` are gone.
nextSteps: Read the four lines under `// Task 4`.
Rename it where it is used too, then do the same for `y`.
Run the file: it should print the same two lines as before.
hints: A variable's name appears where it is made and everywhere it is used.
If you rename it in one place only, Node stops with an error that names the one it no longer knows. Read it: it tells you which line to fix.
Four places change: the two lines that make `x` and `y`, and the two `console.log` lines that use them.
